article_title: Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education
citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Writing-focused GenAI declaration structure with six activity categories
description: A declaration form for writing-focused activities (e.g., a short literature review on technology and society) organised around six activity categories: Planning & Structure, Textual Content Generation, Research & Analysis, Revision & Polish, Visual Content, and Evaluation & Feedback. For each category students (1) state whether GenAI was used (Yes/No), (2) specify the extent of use (Minor, Moderate, Extensive), and (3) provide a short explanation with example prompts. The categories operationalise aspects of the Bouvier et al. taxonomy in an essay-writing context, e.g., "Textual Content Generationaligns withGenerate".
requirements: Students complete per-category Yes/No use, extent rating, and short explanations with example prompts
constraints: Categories were derived from a computing-education activity taxonomy; the article notes the boundary of what counts as GenAI use is not always obvious to students
target_learners: Higher education students completing writing-focused assessments such as professional or literature-review style reports
target_learning_goals: Transparent disclosure of GenAI use in writing tasks
Distinguishing acceptable assistance (e.g., limited revision support) from outsourcing of core content
examples: Planning & Structure covers brainstorming ideas, outlining sections, and structuring arguments; Revision & Polish covers grammar and spelling checks, rephrasing, and formatting citations
key_sources: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef

article_title: Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing
citation: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598
title: Write–Challenge–Defend–Improve cyclical interaction loop
description: The system's user interaction follows a cyclical four-phase model: the student writes an essay, selects a critical persona and receives structured inquiry-based questions with no evaluative language, writes a reflective defense for each question, and only after the defense clears the reflection gate unlocks a concrete revision suggestion and writing tip built on the student's own reasoning. The student then incorporates these into the draft and may re-enter the loop with revised text. The article states the loop is designed so that "cognitive effort always precedes the delivery of suggestions, ensuring the student remains the primary agent of revision."
requirements: A persona selection step and a reflection gate between the Defend and Improve phases
constraints: Optimized for argumentative/persuasive essays; other genres would require redesigning the parsing heuristics and question taxonomies
target_learners: students preparing for argumentative writing assessments
examples: The demo mode mirrors the full loop offline with a pre-loaded middle-school essay about driverless cars and pre-baked questions, defenses coaching, and unlock suggestions for all six question types
key_sources: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598

article_title: Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial
citation: Subigya K. Nepal, Serena Soh, Noah Vinoya, SoHyun Park, Mahnaz Roshanaei, and Gabriella Harari. 2027. Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial. In Proceedings of CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19635
title: Write prompt rules you can verify from transcripts and then verify them; budget decision demands and accept a declined decision
description: The paper distills its audit into two design rules for reflection agents. First, "write prompt rules you can verify from transcripts, and then verify them", because manner rules can fail in nearly every conversation without anyone noticing. Second, it yields "a concrete design rule for reflection agents: budget decision demands and accept it when a participant declines to decide", since repeated demands to decide were the behavior tied to greater career doubt while flattery showed no link to any outcome.
requirements: A deployment that logs complete conversation transcripts so rules can be checked after the fact
constraints: The decision-demand association is observational, so the design rule rests on the most likely explanation the data offer rather than a tested causal effect
target_learners: emerging adults in career reflection programs
examples: The trial's agent doubled closure moves per participant between studies (4.8 to 10.1) and re-posed demands after 15.3% of non-decision answers, producing the corpus's weakest commitments at 3.82 certainty
key_sources: Subigya K. Nepal, Serena Soh, Noah Vinoya, SoHyun Park, Mahnaz Roshanaei, and Gabriella Harari. 2027. Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial. In Proceedings of CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19635

article_title: WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays
citation: Adnan Labib, Yixuan Huang, Jiahui Wu, John Maurice Gayed, Zheng Yuan, Qiao Wang. (2026). WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524
title: WrAFT: deployable modular AWE system with interactive UI for in-line corrective edits and anchored comments
description: WrAFT (Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool) is a modular LLM-powered automated writing evaluation system for argumentative essays, combining a fine-tuned GPT-4o scoring module, a GPT-4o surface-level feedback module, and Claude 3.7 macro and micro deep-level feedback pipelines. Its interactive UI shows a predicted score, a surface-level tab with three display modes including track-changes, and a deep-level tab modeled after Microsoft Word's Comment feature with color-coded highlights. The article states "An interactive user interface has been developed for the system, publicly available and free to use", with a deployable code package on GitHub and a web application at wraft.net.
requirements: Relies on commercial API services (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7), which the article notes raises potential scalability issues related to cost, rate limits, and long-term sustainability
constraints: Developed and tested exclusively on argumentative essays with writing prompts; feedback is solely in English; instances of LLM hallucinations identifying non-existent errors were observed
target_learning_goals: higher-order writing skills such as coherence and argumentation
examples: The final architecture selected the fine-tuned GPT-4o model for scoring, direct prompting with GPT-4o for surface-level feedback, and Claude 3.7 for both deep-level pipelines.
key_sources: Adnan Labib, Yixuan Huang, Jiahui Wu, John Maurice Gayed, Zheng Yuan, Qiao Wang. (2026). WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524

article_title: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era
citation: Smith, Dalton Ross; Whittington, Wilburn; Martinez, Alejandro; Duncan, Aidan; Li, Gang. (2026). A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11540
title: Four-pillar competency rubric: digital/AI literacy, CPS fluency, human-machine collaboration, data-driven decision making
description: Each WRL stage is evaluated along four conceptually distinct pillars: "digital and AI literacy, cyber-physical systems fluency, human-machine collaboration, and data-driven decision making". Pillars were synthesized from Industry 4.0 competency literature and refined to foreground AI-specific competencies; each pillar carries anchored stage examples so the same construct is evidenced differently at WRL 2 versus WRL 7. Scoring pillars separately lets the no-thin-pillar rule detect lopsided profiles such as a strong coder who cannot read an SPC chart.
requirements: Exactly four pillars are retained to keep the rubric manageable for two raters and a single-page transcript while keeping the domains non-overlapping
constraints: The four-pillar partition is a design assumption, not a validated factor structure; establishing the number and statistical independence of the dimensions would require a construct-validity study such as confirmatory factor analysis
target_learning_goals: information-side, machine-side, human-side, and decision-side manufacturing competencies
examples: P2 stage examples run from locating a PLC and its I/O modules at WRL 2 to architecting an OPC-UA-streamed digital twin and resolving a latency incident at WRL 7+
key_sources: Smith, Dalton Ross; Whittington, Wilburn; Martinez, Alejandro; Duncan, Aidan; Li, Gang. (2026). A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11540

article_title: Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry
citation: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a
title: Writing Assessment Scale for audience-directed science writing
description: A researcher-developed 17-item scale assessing students' end-of-unit writing tasks, with each item scored on a 3-point scale (unsatisfactory, satisfactory, very satisfactory). Items address letter structure, grammar, clarity, fluency, conceptual content, use of everyday language, examples, visual representations, and appropriateness for the intended audience. Items concerning language and expression, content, and audience were combined into a total writing score; inter-rater agreement was 94% with Cohen's kappa of 0.89.
requirements: Scoring by raters experienced in assessing student writing until consensus
Random selection of writing samples for inter-rater reliability checking
constraints: The article notes a limitation that groups were compared on writing scores without controlling students' prewriting scores, so prior writing ability was not accounted for
examples: Six items (5-10) related to conceptual understanding were combined separately, revealing that younger-student and peer writers demonstrated significantly better understanding on writing than teacher-directed writers
key_sources: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a

article_title: Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality
citation: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3
title: Writing Lab six-lesson lesson-series pattern alternating divergent and convergent thinking with a fixed compare-contrast, generate, select, apply, evaluate activity cycle
description: A reusable lesson-series pattern for creative writing in upper secondary education: a metacognitive introductory lesson, four element-focused lessons (mindmaps/character, suspense, dialogue, perspective), and a final application lesson. "Lessons two through five followed a similar pattern: alternate divergent and convergent thinking, compare and contrast, application and evaluation." Cognitive strategy instruction follows Merrill's demonstration and application principles, using strong and weak peer models for observational learning, extensive drafting phases (about 20 of 50 minutes in four lessons), and group peer feedback with compliments and recommendations rather than competition.
requirements: Alternation must be explicitly indicated to students (icons in materials) and contextualized to the lesson's target writing task
A writer-reader community with constructive, encouraging peer feedback and a safe climate where nothing is considered crazy or stupid
constraints: Designed for a context with no existing creative writing lesson series for upper secondary education in the Netherlands; the program deliberately did not address transfer to argumentative writing explicitly
target_learners: Grade 10 pre-university secondary students in Dutch L1 education
target_learning_goals: Drafting and rewriting creative short stories
Creative thinking strategies (fluency, originality, flexibility, elaboration)
examples: Lesson 4 ('Roaring, whispering, screeching, or panting?') generates sentence variations divergently, shares them whole-class, expands with tags, drafts a dialogue-based story, and acts dialogues out in groups
key_sources: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3

article_title: The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning
citation: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3
title: Writing-system account: sound-to-symbol mapping transparency and the range of monitored cognitive processes shape metacognitive monitoring of visually presented word learning
description: The article proposes that the writing system a person uses modulates metacognitive monitoring of word learning in the visual but not the auditory modality. It states that "the presence and transparency of sound-to-symbol mapping influences the success of word acquisition and the self-evaluation (metacognition) of word learning, when words are visually presented." Opaque mapping (Arabic abjad) hinders transfer of metacognitive skills from the auditory baseline to the visual modality, while the logographic Chinese script, lacking phoneme-to-symbol mapping, trains metacognition because learners must simultaneously monitor strategies for inferring both pronunciation and semantics of each character.
requirements: Learners must have literacy experience in a specific writing system, since the account rests on inculturated processing of written information
constraints: The account concerns metacognition measured via retrospective confidence ratings, i.e. processes related to conscious awareness; the authors note observed population differences may in principle be cultural rather than linguistic, though they argue the modality-specific pattern supports a linguistic origin
target_learners: University students aged 18-30 who are native speakers of Portuguese, Arabic or Mandarin Chinese learning foreign-language vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Inferential (incidental, context-based) vocabulary learning and accurate self-evaluation of word-learning success
examples: Arabic speakers showed lower metacognitive sensitivity in the visual than auditory modality; Chinese speakers showed the highest visual-modality metacognition, attributed to monitoring multiple cognitive strategies for pronunciation and semantics of logographic characters
key_sources: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3

article_title: The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the United States: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Aitken, A. A., Graham, S., Cao, Y., & Nusrat, A. (2026). The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the United States: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10197-6
title: Writers-within-community (WWC) model of writing
description: The writers-within-community model holds that "writing takes place because of the reciprocal relationship between the writer's cognitive resources and the sociocultural context in which writing occurs". It positions the writer, with cognitive and linguistic resources such as attention, working memory, knowledge, and beliefs, as embedded in a layered system of community influences from immediate goals and tools to classroom norms and broader institutional forces. The model served as the theoretical foundation of this meta-analysis and guided how outcomes were grouped into constructs (transcription, translation, output, writing beliefs) and how treatments were coded as writer-focused, community-focused, or both.
requirements: Writing is understood as situated in a community context; analysis of writing instruction must account for both writer-side cognitive and linguistic resources and community-side influences such as classroom norms and institutional factors.
constraints: The article notes that practices found effective in other countries or contexts may not yield the same outcomes in U.S. classrooms, so evidence must be situated within the social, cultural, and institutional features of U.S. schools.
target_learners: K-12 English language learners in the United States
target_learning_goals: Writing performance, including writing quality, transcription, translation, output, and writing beliefs
examples: The meta-analysis grouped narrow measures (e.g., spelling, grammar errors, words written) into WWC-aligned constructs and coded interventions as targeting writer-focused processes, community-focused supports, or both.
key_sources: Aitken, A. A., Graham, S., Cao, Y., & Nusrat, A. (2026). The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the United States: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10197-6

article_title: Writing Self-Efficacy in Postsecondary Students: a Scoping Review
citation: Kim M. Mitchell, Sharon Zumbrunn, Danielle N. Berry, Lisa Demczuk. (2023). Writing Self-Efficacy in Postsecondary Students: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09798-2
title: Writing self-efficacy as beliefs about writing ability within Bandura's social cognitive framework of triadic reciprocality
description: The review organizes writing self-efficacy research within Bandura's social cognitive framework, defining writing self-efficacy as "a learner's beliefs about their ability to write" and situating it in triadic reciprocality, where learning depends on reciprocal interactions among thoughts, behaviors, and environment. On this view, writing self-efficacy beliefs influence perseverance, academic choices, and performance, while social and contextual factors such as feedback and instructional conditions shape the beliefs in turn. The review uses this framework to justify its focus on writing contexts and pedagogy.
requirements: Studies must employ a self-efficacy measure specific to writing rather than a general academic self-efficacy measure
constraints: The review excluded reflective, blog, and creative writing contexts, focusing only on academic writing in postsecondary English-language settings
target_learning_goals: writing ability and writing success in academic contexts
key_sources: Kim M. Mitchell, Sharon Zumbrunn, Danielle N. Berry, Lisa Demczuk. (2023). Writing Self-Efficacy in Postsecondary Students: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09798-2

article_title: The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children’s Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study
citation: Skar, G. B., Graham, S., & Huebener, A. (2023). The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children's Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09729-1
title: Writer(s)-within-Community (WWC) model of writing development
description: The Writer(s)-within-Community model (Graham, 2018a, 2018b) is the theoretical framework that guided both the prior first-grade study and this longitudinal replication. The article states that "The WWC proposed that writing development is simultaneously and interactively shaped and bound by where it is learned and the cognitive capabilities and resources of those learning to write." This framing motivated restricting the study to a single country (Norway), since writing instruction is shaped by unique cultural, social, institutional, political, and historical factors. The model also motivated the choice of measures: attitude toward writing fuels effort, while limited cognitive resources make slow transcription skills such as handwriting interfere with conceptualization and ideation for beginning writers.
requirements: Assessment of writing should capture motivation (attitude), transcription resources (handwriting fluency), and the end product (text quality), as the model treats these as interacting components
constraints: The model led the authors to focus on a single country, since the teaching of writing in any single country is influenced by its own unique cultural, social, institutional, political, and historical factors
examples: The model guided the assessment of attitude toward writing, handwriting fluency, and overall writing quality in Norwegian first- and second-graders
key_sources: Skar, G. B., Graham, S., & Huebener, A. (2023). The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children's Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09729-1

article_title: Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading–writing relations, and dynamic relations as a function of measurement/dimensions of written composition.
citation: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564
title: Multidimensional written composition scoring protocol: writing quality, writing productivity, and correctness in writing from two expository prompts
description: The study assessed written composition with two expository prompts (the WIAT-III Essay Composition task and an experimental Beaver source-based prompt, 15 minutes each) and scored compositions on three dimensions. "Writing quality was operationalized as the extent and clarity of idea development and organization" on a 1-to-7 modified 6+1 Trait rubric (kappa .87–.95); writing productivity was the number of words written (agreement .95); and correctness in writing used the CBM correct minus incorrect word sequences (CIWS) score (similarity coefficients .94–.95). Spelling was corrected for quality and productivity scoring but handwritten versions were used for correctness scoring.
requirements: Typed-up versions with corrected spelling are needed for quality and productivity evaluation because spelling errors and handwriting legibility influence evaluators' judgments.
constraints: Compositions that were mostly verbatim copies of the source text were scored zero (six students' compositions on the Beaver prompt).
target_learning_goals: Assessment of written composition across quality, productivity, and correctness dimensions
examples: Children wrote about their favorite game (WIAT-III) and about beavers after reading an illustrated 297-word passage, with 15 minutes per prompt.
key_sources: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564

article_title: Not Fade Away?
citation: Devedzic, V. (2016). Not Fade Away? Commentary to paper Education and The Semantic Web (IJAIED Vol.14, 2004). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 378–386. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0051-2
title: Wrap Semantic Web infrastructure into valued learning products rather than selling it as infrastructure
description: The article's central design recommendation: "Linked Data can only be the infrastructure, and infrastructure never sells as such." The way to sell Semantic Web in education is to follow the Google Knowledge Graph and Facebook Open Graph Protocol approach — enrich another valued idea, technology, or category of learning systems and resources (PLEs, OERs, MOOCs, learning analytics) with ontologies, semantic search and Web of data, so the technologies work in the background.
requirements: A valued learning system, product or resource category to enrich with Semantic technologies
constraints: The commentary warns Linked Data still poses practical challenges in education: data quality/correctness/completeness, community agreement on vocabularies, source stability, and annotation difficulty
target_learners: developers and researchers building educational systems
target_learning_goals: adoption and practical impact of Semantic technologies in education
examples: Google Knowledge Graph uses Linked Data principles and Schema.org vocabularies but sells knowledge and easier navigation wrapped in ordinary search results; Facebook users see OGP metadata effects without knowing OGP exists
key_sources: Devedzic, V. (2016). Not Fade Away? Commentary to paper Education and The Semantic Web (IJAIED Vol.14, 2004). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 378–386. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0051-2

article_title: Evaluating the Impact of Learner Control and Interactivity in Conversational Tutoring Systems for Persuasive Writing
citation: Wambsganss, T., Benke, I., Maedche, A., Koedinger, K., & Käser, T. (2025). Evaluating the Impact of Learner Control and Interactivity in Conversational Tutoring Systems for Persuasive Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00409-x
title: WritingTutor: a conversational tutoring system for persuasive essay writing with learner control features.
description: WritingTutor is a web-based conversational tutoring system that guides students through persuasive essay-writing exercises via dialog-based interaction, providing theory input and adaptive feedback on essay objectivity, polarity, and text quality. It comprises a learner-centered conversational user interface, distinct learner control features (content navigation buttons and an interface appearance panel for avatar, name, color scheme, and background), and an NLP/ML back end using a Naive Bayes classifier with semantic similarity matching for intent classification and the textblob library for polarity and objectivity feedback.
requirements: A Naive Bayes classifier trained on labeled user intents (62 intents) with a confidence threshold of 0.70, plus textblob for polarity/objectivity scoring.
constraints: Designed and evaluated for persuasive essay writing with university students; the article notes findings indicate limitations of learner control embedded in CTS.
key_sources: Wambsganss, T., Benke, I., Maedche, A., Koedinger, K., & Käser, T. (2025). Evaluating the Impact of Learner Control and Interactivity in Conversational Tutoring Systems for Persuasive Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00409-x

article_title: Reflections on educational technology research and development
citation: Jonathan Michael Spector. (2017). Reflections on educational technology research and development. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9545-y
title: Write and talk to be understood: use simple, descriptive language
description: The author argues, from 15 years as ETR&D Development Editor and his philosophy training, that the basic goal of communication is to be understood, and that simple, descriptive language promotes understanding. He cites Nielsen's 'A Game of India' as an example of 'a complex story using only the simplest, descriptive language'. He offers the 4 Cs of effective communication: compelling, clear, coherent and concise.
requirements: The communication should have something of interest and value to say, told as a compelling story with evident purpose and scope
constraints: The author notes some remarks may seem disconnected and unnecessarily personal
examples: The author shared Nielsen's 'A Game of India' with students as an example of good writing
key_sources: Jonathan Michael Spector. (2017). Reflections on educational technology research and development. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9545-y

article_title: The Significance of Journal Writing in Improving Listening and Reading Comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA)
citation: Ina Saad, Magdi Ahmed. (2015). The Significance of Journal Writing in Improving Listening and Reading Comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11): 815-821. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031106
title: Language-production account of why journal writing improves comprehension: writing makes learners creators of language rather than passive recipients
description: The article's Correlation Justification section offers a mechanism account for the observed comprehension gains: in reading and listening, students "tend to be passive learners of the language whereas in writing they are creators of the language who use multiple cognitive processes of language production." Supporting mechanisms include listening-based tasks requiring comprehension before writing, looking up topic-specific vocabulary and cultural expressions to support viewpoints, structural sentence formation in meaningful contexts, and a proposed chain in which reading ability enhances listening ability. The section also cites claimed benefits of active involvement, critical thinking, and an alternative communication channel for students reluctant to speak.
requirements: Journal tasks must be closely connected to the topics and concepts taught during the school day for the reinforcement effect the authors describe
constraints: The authors present these as possible logical reasons explaining the observed patterns, not as experimentally tested mechanisms
target_learning_goals: critical and analytical thinking in the target language
examples: The authors liken the reading-to-listening enhancement chain to reactions in Newton's Cradle collision balls, especially in Arabic where accurate reading of a word or phrase expands recognition of it in both reading and listening
key_sources: Ina Saad, Magdi Ahmed. (2015). The Significance of Journal Writing in Improving Listening and Reading Comprehension in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11): 815-821. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031106

article_title: Writing-Reading Relationships: Effectiveness of Writing Activities as Pre-Reading Tasks to Enhance L2 Inferential Reading Comprehension
citation: Wickramaarachchi, T.I. (2014). Writing-Reading Relationships: Effectiveness of Writing Activities as Pre-Reading Tasks to Enhance L2 Inferential Reading Comprehension. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.5p.213
title: Writing-based pre-reading (prw) task
description: The prw task is the study's independent variable: "the readers writing about a certain topic before they read a passage on the topic". It combines writing, reading and schema activation, drawing on the rationale that pre-reading tasks prepare and motivate students to read and that writing about one's own experience related to a topic activates background knowledge. In the intervention, the experimental group received a prw task prior to each of six reading passages while the control group performed the tasks without the pre-reading component.
requirements: A topic is provided before the reading passage so students write about it prior to reading
Reading passages on the same topic follow the writing activity
constraints: The study tested it only for inferential comprehension with lower-intermediate ESL undergraduates in one setting
target_learners: first-year ESL undergraduates at lower intermediate proficiency
examples: Over 6 one-hour sessions, the experimental group completed a prw task before each reading passage and MCQ set
key_sources: Wickramaarachchi, T.I. (2014). Writing-Reading Relationships: Effectiveness of Writing Activities as Pre-Reading Tasks to Enhance L2 Inferential Reading Comprehension. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.5p.213

article_title: The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety
citation: Nihat BAYAT. (2014). The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.3.1720
title: Writing Apprehension Test (Daly & Miller, 1975; Turkish adaptation)
description: The study measured writing anxiety with "the Writing Apprehension Test developed by Daly and Miller (1975)", adapted to Turkish by Zorbaz (2010). It is a 26-item, 5-point Likert scale in which negative statements are inverted and total scores indicate anxiety level, with low scores desirable. The adapted scale showed Cronbach's alpha of .901 with second-stage primary school students and .938 with university students in a reliability study by Tiryaki (2011), which the article cites as evidence it is sufficiently valid and reliable for this use.
requirements: Scores from negative statements are inverted before computing the total score
constraints: The reported reliability coefficients come from other samples (primary school and university students) rather than this study's own participants
target_learning_goals: measuring writing anxiety as an affective outcome of writing instruction
examples: Administered to both groups at the beginning of the research in a session lasting approximately 30 minutes, then again after the 10-week experimental procedures

article_title: Best Management Practice for Understanding Learning in Sustainable Water Resource Management (WRM) for Secondary Science Teachers in Thailand

article_title: Teaching Research Skills to Undergraduate Students Using an Active Learning Approach: A Proposed Model for Preparatory-Year Students in Saudi Arabia
citation: Hamdan Alghamdi, A. K., & Deraney, P. (2018). Teaching Research Skills to Undergraduate Students Using an Active Learning Approach: A Proposed Model for Preparatory-Year Students in Saudi Arabia. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 30(2), 184-194. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/
title: Writing and Research course covering 14 skills through five broad aspects of learning
description: The writing and research (WR) course is a required first-year course in the Saudi preparatory program culminating in a 3,500-5,000-word research paper. The instructor emphasized five broad aspects of learning, including "the requirement for cooperation, mutual support, and teamwork" and "the appropriate utilization of technology in order to find an answer." Through these five areas, 14 writing and research skills (Table 1) are covered, ranging from differentiating qualitative and quantitative research types to designing appropriate research tools. Student mastery was measured by a 20-question multiple-choice final exam checked for content validity by professionals in ESL and education.
requirements: Students must complete the foundational preparatory year English language program or IELTS level 5.0 in writing before enrollment
constraints: The study was conducted on the women's campus only because education is gender segregated in Saudi Arabia
target_learners: female undergraduates ages 18-21 with Arabic as a first language in a Saudi preparatory year
target_learning_goals: academic research skills such as writing proposals, literature reviews, hypotheses, and APA-formatted papers
examples: Sample student research topics included the effect of text language on academic writing and the choice for female students between marriage and higher education

article_title: Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks
citation: Weston-Sementelli, J. L., Allen, L. K., & McNamara, D. S. (2016). Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0127-7
title: Writing Pal intelligent tutoring system provides explicit writing strategy instruction with game-based practice and automated writing evaluation
description: The Writing Pal is an intelligent tutoring system designed to provide explicit instruction on writing strategies and opportunities to practice writing and receive feedback, specifically targeting persuasive essays similar to standardized test tasks. Instruction includes "a series of nine strategy instruction modules, covering freewriting, planning, introduction building, body building, conclusion building, cohesion building, and revision", delivered via 5-10 minute lesson videos with animated characters and checkpoint quizzes. Students practice through over a dozen game-based activities plus an automated writing evaluation (AWE) component that provides summative and formative feedback on drafted essays.
requirements: The system is designed to be modular, allowing educators and researchers to utilize only the modules they deem necessary
constraints: The Writing Pal is designed to target the writing of persuasive essays, which differ from source-based essays in that they do not require the usage of source materials
target_learners: students preparing for standardized writing assessments
examples: The present study capitalized on the modular aspect of the Writing Pal to select nine videos and three games from four modules (Planning, Introduction Building, Body Building, Conclusion Building) relevant to source-based writing

article_title: The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt
citation: Ashraf Atta M. S. Salem. (2013). The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt. English Language Teaching, 6(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n7p33
title: Introduce the writing workshop approach in faculties of education for teaching writing
description: The article recommends adopting the writing workshop approach, defined as "a process-based approach for teaching writing in a meaningful environment", in teacher education. It involves mini-lessons, writing and rewriting stages, and sharing time with the teacher as guide and facilitator. The recommendation follows the study's significant pre-post gains in basic writing skills.
requirements: Teacher acts as guide and facilitator rather than lecturer
Program includes mini-lessons, sustained writing time, and sharing/celebration sessions
constraints: Study conducted without a control group in one Egyptian faculty of education
target_learners: Third-year primary stage prospective teachers of English
target_learning_goals: Basic writing skills (mechanics of writing): process writing, punctuation, spelling
examples: Forty prospective teachers were taught with the workshop program for eight weeks, two two-hour sessions per week, and significantly improved their basic writing test scores.

article_title: The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt
citation: Ashraf Atta M. S. Salem. (2013). The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt. English Language Teaching, 6(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n7p33
title: Writing workshop as a student-centered, process-based approach to teaching writing
description: The writing workshop is defined in the article as "a process-based approach for teaching writing in a meaningful environment" that teaches writing in a social context. It typically begins with a mini-lesson, followed by writing and rewriting stages, and ends with a sharing or celebration time such as an author's chair. The teacher serves as a guide and facilitator, and the framework highlights the active role of the learner, the social nature of writing, and the recursive rather than linear nature of the writing process.
requirements: Mini-lesson at the beginning of the session
Sustained writing and rewriting time
Sharing/celebration time for students to present work
Teacher acting as guide and facilitator
constraints: When implemented in ideal form, writing workshops take a large portion of the instructional day
examples: The researcher built an eight-week program on this framework with two two-hour sessions per week for prospective English teachers in Egypt.

article_title: Neighbourhood effects on educational attainment. What matters more: Exposure to poverty or exposure to affluence?
citation: Troost, A. A., van Ham, M., & Manley, D. J. (2023). Neighbourhood effects on educational attainment. What matters more: Exposure to poverty or exposure to affluence? PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281928
title: Wright's three theoretical approaches to social inequality as a lens on neighbourhood effects research
description: The article uses Wright's typology of three theoretical approaches within the sociology of class, social mobility and inequality to explain why neighbourhood effects research overlooks affluence. The individual-attributes approach focuses on meritocratic resources shaping life chances; the Weberian opportunity hoarding approach studies how higher strata protect access to prestigious positions via economic, cultural and social capital and exclusion mechanisms; and the Marxist approach analyses domination and exploitation. The article argues quantitative neighbourhood effects research mixes the first two, and that Bourdieu's social and cultural capital concepts implicitly embody opportunity hoarding, so studying poverty in isolation disregards affluent social actors.
requirements: Applying the framework requires conceptualising neighbourhood mechanisms in terms of the presence of various forms of capital rather than a lack of it, as the article recommends
constraints: The article notes middle-range quantitative study structures usually do not allow extensive theoretical commentary about inequality, so the framework is applied selectively
target_learners: children and adolescents in segregated urban neighbourhoods
target_learning_goals: understanding how spatially concentrated affluence and poverty shape educational attainment and the reproduction of socioeconomic inequality
examples: The article frames its finding that affluent neighbours' effect outweighs poverty's effect as support for the opportunity hoarding view that the rich are rich in part because the poor are poor
key_sources: Troost, A. A., van Ham, M., & Manley, D. J. (2023). Neighbourhood effects on educational attainment. What matters more: Exposure to poverty or exposure to affluence? PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281928
